{{Short description|German-American mathematical physicist (1932–2024)}}
[[File:Ray-Sachs-Ivor-Robinson-Art-Komar-and-John-Lighton-Synge-Jablonna-1962-Photo.png|thumb|''From left:'' Rainer Sachs, [[Ivor Robinson (physicist)|Ivor Robinson]], [[Arthur Komar|Art Komar]], [[John Lighton Synge]], in 1962]]
'''Rainer Kurt''' "'''Ray'''" '''Sachs''' (June 13, 1932 – April 16, 2024) was a German-American mathematical physicist, with interests in general relativistic cosmology and astrophysics, as well as a computational radiation biologist. He was professor emeritus of Mathematics and Physics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and adjunct professor at [[Tufts University School of Medicine|Tufts Medical School]].<ref name="CV" />

== Early life ==
Sachs was born in [[Frankfurt am Main]] on June 13, 1932, a son of the German Jewish metallurgist [[George Sachs]]. In 1937 the family left Germany to flee from Nazi persecution, and settled in the [[United States]], so Rainer Sachs is generally considered an American scientist. In 1949, he graduated from [[University School (Ohio)|University School]], in [[Cleveland]], Ohio.

He received his bachelor's degree in mathematics from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] in 1953 and his PhD in theoretical physics from [[Syracuse University]] in 1959.<ref name="CV">[http://math.berkeley.edu/~sachs/cv.html Sachs Curriculum Vitae]</ref>

== Career ==
In 1962, [[Joshua N. Goldberg]] and Sachs proved the [[Goldberg–Sachs theorem]]. Later that year, he gave the first exposition of the asymptotically flat spacetime symmetry group, which he called the "generalized Bondi-Metzner group" and is now known as the [[Bondi–Metzner–Sachs group]].<ref name="sachs1962">{{cite journal|title=Asymptotic symmetries in gravitational theory|journal=Physical Review|volume=128|pages=2851–2864|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.128.2851|year=1962|last1=Sachs|first1=R.|issue=6|bibcode=1962PhRv..128.2851S}}</ref>

In 1966, he and [[Ronald Kantowski]] were responsible for the [[Kantowski–Sachs metric|Kantowski–Sachs]] [[dust solution]]s to the [[Einstein field equation]].<ref>{{cite journal | author=Kantowski, R.| author2=  Sachs, R. K.| name-list-style= amp | title=Some spatially homogeneous anisotropic dust models | journal=J. Math. Phys. | date=1966 | volume=7 | pages=443 | doi=10.1063/1.1704952|bibcode = 1966JMP.....7..443K | issue=3 }}</ref> These are a widely used family of [[anisotropic cosmology|anisotropic cosmological models]].

In 1967, he and [[Arthur M. Wolfe]] were the authors of the [[Sachs–Wolfe effect]], which concerns a property of the [[cosmic microwave background]] radiation.<ref>
{{cite journal
 |last1=Sachs |first1=R. K. 
 |last2=Wolfe |first2=A. M. 
 |date=1967 
 |title=Perturbations of a Cosmological Model and Angular Variations of the Microwave Background 
 |journal=[[Astrophysical Journal]]
 |volume=147 |page=73 
 |doi=10.1086/148982 |bibcode=1967ApJ...147...73S
}}</ref> The [[Ehlers–Geren–Sachs theorem]], published in 1968 by [[Jürgen Ehlers]], P. Geren and R. Sachs, shows that if, in a given universe, there exists a reference frame at each event such that the cosmic background radiation is isotropic, then under certain conditions that universe is an isotropic and homogeneous [[FLRW]] spacetime.

From 1969 to 1993, he was a Professor of Mathematics and Physics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] (UCB), and from 1993 he was Professor Emeritus at UCB. In 1994, he was appointed Research Professor of Mathematics UCB, and since 2005 he has been an adjunct professor at the Tufts medical school.

Until 1985, he worked on [[General relativity|general relativistic]] [[cosmology]] and [[astrophysics]]. With Hung-Hsi Wu, he co-wrote the books ''General Relativity and Cosmology'' in 1971<ref>R. K. Sachs and H. Wu (Italian Physical Society), G''eneral Relativity and Cosmology''. Academic Press Incorporated, U.S. (August 1971).</ref> and ''General Relativity for Mathematicians'' in 1977.<ref>[http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1977grm..book.....S General Relativity for Mathematicians, Sachs, R. K.; Wu, H. -H., 1977].</ref>
From 1985, he has worked in mathematical and [[computational biology]], especially radiation biology. His work in radiobiology has included research on radiation and cancer.<ref>[http://www.pnas.org/cgi/reprint/2235592100v1.pdf Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences].</ref>

== Later life ==
Sachs died on April 16, 2024, at the age of 91 in Berkeley, California.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Remembering Rainer Sachs {{!}} Physics |url=https://physics.berkeley.edu/news/remembering-rainer-sachs |access-date=2024-06-12 |website=physics.berkeley.edu}}</ref>
